articles.body: A candidate I interviewed in October had a bullet that read "Leveraged AI to increase team productivity by 300%." I asked the obvious question: 300% of what, measured how? He went quiet, then explained that he had set up Copilot for his team and people "felt faster". He was a good engineer. That one bullet cost him more credibility in five minutes than the rest of his resume had earned. The next candidate wrote: "Built an LLM-assisted test scaffolding script; cut time to first passing test on new Laravel modules from ~2 days to ~half a day across 9 modules (measured from PR timestamps)." I spent ten minutes asking her about it, and every answer made her stronger. I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every example and rewrite myself.

articles.title: I made a small browser tool to shrink chat photos and remove metadata
articles.excerpt: I send photos through WhatsApp and Telegram pretty often, and I've always found two things annoying. One is the file size. A photo from my phone can easily be 5 MB or more, which feels unnecessary whe…
articles.body: I send photos through WhatsApp and Telegram pretty often, and I've always found two things annoying. One is the file size. A photo from my phone can easily be 5 MB or more, which feels unnecessary when I'm just sending someone a picture in a chat. Some apps compress photos automatically, but the results aren't always great. Others have upload limits, and large files can be a pain on a slow connection. The other thing is metadata. Photos taken on a phone can contain GPS coordinates, the phone model, the date and time they were taken, and other EXIF information. Most people probably don't think about this when sharing photos. I didn't pay much attention to it either until I started looking into how much information a single image file can carry. Why not just use an online compressor?

articles.title: Snapshotting a DigitalOcean Droplet while it's running
articles.excerpt: DigitalOcean lets you snapshot a Droplet while it's running, and its docs are careful about it. They say a live snapshot "may result in performance degradation and compromise data consistency", and th…
articles.body: DigitalOcean lets you snapshot a Droplet while it's running, and its docs are careful about it. They say a live snapshot "may result in performance degradation and compromise data consistency", and that many databases only guarantee a consistent disk if you stop them or power the Droplet off first. That's sensible advice. I wanted to know what it means in practice: what a snapshot of a busy Droplet contains when you restore it, whether the Droplet slows down while it's taken, and what powering off first actually costs you. The setup One Droplet in Frankfurt, the 2 GB / 1 vCPU size with a 50 GB disk, running Ubuntu 24.04 and Postgres 16 with its default settings. On it, two writers ran the whole time: Postgres. One numbered row per transaction, about 100 a second.

articles.title: Poseidon: Monitoring a Simulated Oilfield with Kafka, Spark and the Elastic Stack
articles.excerpt: Introduction Oil and gas operations generate large volumes of industrial data, collected continuously from sensors, equipment and production systems across wells and facilities. Turning this data into…
articles.body: Introduction Oil and gas operations generate large volumes of industrial data, collected continuously from sensors, equipment and production systems across wells and facilities. Turning this data into actionable insights requires reliable ingestion, processing and analytics. To address this challenge, I built DatAbde, my own data platform, and used it to develop Poseidon, an oil and gas project that addresses these industry challenges through a simulated oilfield. Using Apache Kafka and Spark, Poseidon processes industrial telemetry through a Medallion-based ETL pipeline, feeding two analytical workflows: near-real-time monitoring with the Elastic Stack, and historical business reporting with Spark, Delta tables on MinIO and Metabase.
articles.author: AJOUHY ABDELAH

articles.title: The First 72 Hours After a Data Breach Goes Public: Legal Clocks, Press, Search Results and Reviews
articles.excerpt: "You have 72 hours" is the most repeated line in breach advice, and it is a half-truth. The number comes from one law, Article 33 of the GDPR. It applies "where feasible." It runs from when you become…
articles.body: "You have 72 hours" is the most repeated line in breach advice, and it is a half-truth. The number comes from one law, Article 33 of the GDPR. It applies "where feasible." It runs from when you become aware of the breach. And it is owed to a regulator, not to your customers. The clock that actually governs your reputation is a different one. It starts when the story is public: a reporter has the file, a researcher posts a screenshot, an attacker lists your data for sale, or a customer opens a letter. Your investigation can still be running when that happens. This post separates the two kinds of clock, sets out what the main rules say in their own words, and then lays out an hour-by-hour plan for the public side: notices, press, search results and reviews.
articles.author: DefendMyRep

articles.title: Jira Timeline vs Plans: What Happens When a Date Moves
articles.excerpt: Just after midnight on 14 November we dragged one work item a week later in a Jira plan on our test site, then read back the two work items waiting on it. Neither had moved. Four days earlier we'd don…
articles.body: Just after midnight on 14 November we dragged one work item a week later in a Jira plan on our test site, then read back the two work items waiting on it. Neither had moved. Four days earlier we'd done the same on the space Timeline (a space is what Jira used to call a project), Jira's built-in Gantt view, a bar chart of work over time, and got the same answer. In both places Jira drew a red line, said the dates overlap, and left the rest to us. So if you're asking "Jira Timeline vs Plans" because you want the dates of blocked work to follow a slip, neither does that when you edit a date by hand. Plans (Atlassian's advanced planning, the feature that used to be called Advanced Roadmaps) has one more tool, the auto-scheduler. It did re-date the whole chain in our test.

articles.title: How I cut 130 KB from every page by lazy-loading one library
articles.excerpt: I run a site with 90+ small browser tools (calculators, QR and barcode generators, image tools). Everything ships in one JavaScript bundle, and during a recent performance audit one thing stood out: a…
articles.body: I run a site with 90+ small browser tools (calculators, QR and barcode generators, image tools). Everything ships in one JavaScript bundle, and during a recent performance audit one thing stood out: a QR-code reading library (jsQR) was inside the main bundle, so every visitor downloaded it, even people who only opened a salary calculator. Moving it out of the main bundle and loading it only on the QR tools cut about 130 KB from every other page. Here is the simple pattern, no framework needed. 1. Find out what is actually heavy Before moving anything, measure. A quick way is to minify the bundle with and without a library and compare sizes, or use a bundle analyzer if you have a build step.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 13, 1971: NASA's Mariner 9 becomes 1st spacecraft to orbit Mars, revealing close looks at the Martian surface
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. At the time, scientists didn't know much about the Red Planet. NASA had several Mars flybys before Mariner 9 . Those flybys showed that Mars had a cratered surface , so some scientists thought that Mars looked just like the moon. Then Mariner 9 blew blew their minds. When Mariner 9 got to Mars , it arrived in the middle of a dust storm. It saw some tall structures sticking through the clouds. When the dust settled, images from Mariner 9 revealed that these structures were the tops of huge volcanoes. One volcano, Olympus Mons , is the tallest in the solar system. Mariner 9 also spotted an enormous canyon called Valles Marineris . This canyon is five times longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona.

articles.body: In many of the biggest science fiction franchises, conversing with alien races is an absolute doddle. articles.title: Think you have good eyesight? Try counting the stars in the Pleiades tonight
articles.excerpt: Every November, I give myself a completely unscientific eyesight test using one of my favorite sights in the night sky — the Pleiades. How many stars can you see?
articles.body: Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand. I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again. This is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky. The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars.

articles.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
articles.excerpt: "SignDrop" exploit lets local users gain all-powerful System rights.
articles.body: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions.
